message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit and two months for an unfurnished unit.
• The deposit must be returned within 30 days after you move out, minus any lawful deductions.
• Landlords must provide a written itemized list of deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Take photos or videos of the unit when you move in and out. | | **Habitability** | • Texas law requires landlords to keep the premises in a habitable condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, structural safety).
• Landlords must repair major defects within a reasonable time after notice. | • Report problems in writing (email or text) and keep a copy.
• If repairs are not made, you may withhold rent or pursue a repair‑and‑deduct claim. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable. | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • Landlords cannot enter the unit without proper notice (usually 24–48 hours) unless it’s an emergency. | • Ask for a written notice of entry and keep a record of any visits. | | **Discrimination** | • Under federal Fair Housing laws and Texas statutes, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. | | **Lease Termination** | • Either party can terminate a lease with proper notice (usually 30 days for month‑to‑month).
• Landlords must provide a written notice of termination. | • Keep a copy of any termination notice. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the Texas eviction procedure (notice, court filing, judgment).
• You have the right to contest an eviction in court. | • Respond promptly to any eviction notice and seek legal counsel if needed. | | **Repair‑and‑Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, but you must follow the proper procedure and keep receipts. | • Document the defect, notify the landlord in writing, and keep all receipts. | | **Right to Privacy** | • Landlords must respect your privacy and cannot conduct searches without a warrant or your consent, except in emergencies. | • Know your lease’s entry clauses and keep a log of any entries. | | **Utilities** | • Landlords must provide essential utilities (water, heat, electricity) unless otherwise specified. | • Verify which utilities are included in your rent. | | **Subletting** | • Texas law does not prohibit subletting, but the lease may restrict it. | • Get written permission from the landlord before subletting. | | **Dispute Resolution** | • Many leases include a mediation or arbitration clause. | • Understand the clause and consider alternative dispute resolution if you prefer. | ### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Look for clauses on rent, security deposit, maintenance, entry, and termination. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written notices, and receipts. 3. **Know the Notice Periods** – 30 days for most lease terminations, 24–48 hours for entry. 4. **Keep Copies of All Correspondence** – Emails, texts, letters. 5. **Know Your Local Resources** – Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs, local tenant‑rights groups, and legal aid clinics. --- #### When to Seek Legal Help - **Unlawful Eviction**: If you receive an eviction notice and believe it’s unjustified. - **Discrimination Claims**: If you suspect the landlord is discriminating. - **Security Deposit Disputes**: If the landlord refuses to return your deposit or provides an unreasonable deduction. - **Habitability Issues**: If major repairs are not made in a timely manner. You can contact the Texas Attorney General’s Office, local legal aid organizations, or a private attorney for assistance. --- **Disclaimer**: This information is for general educational purposes only and does not constitute legal advice. For specific legal questions, consult a qualified attorney.
